clue.text: Musical lines on a northern isle

parts.note: the five lines music is written on are the staff or stave

explanation.surface: Music being played or written on a remote Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: STAFFA is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland, home of Fingal's Cave, which inspired Mendelssohn's overture, so the musical surface fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffa is an islet of the Inner Hebrides, off the coast of Scotland, so it lies in the far north of Britain.

parts.note: a book about one's own life has the writer as its subject, referred to in the first person throughout; subject also means topic

explanation.surface: The topic an autobiography deals with.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as THE ME: the subject of a life written by oneself is oneself, while the whole word means a topic.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic or subject is the main idea of a work; in an autobiography the subject is the writer, 'me'.

parts.note: bust reads as a sculpted head but also as broken: the bits of something smashed

explanation.surface: The parts of a sculpture of a head and shoulders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' as a statue suggests a sculpture's features; as an adjective, 'bust' means broken, so its pieces are the broken bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Small broken-off pieces of something smashed are shards or bits.

parts.note: as means like, in the sense of in the manner of
eight English monarchs were named Henry, so a Henry is an example of a king

explanation.surface: Someone as demanding as King Henry, such as Henry VIII.
explanation.definitionFit: Demanding is requesting or requiring, the same as inquiring for or requesting.

clue.text: Put down an Australian town with an English city — an ancient one : good man!

parts.note: Bath is a spa city in Somerset, England
Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia, the usual crossword ancient city
a saint is a good man, abbreviated St

explanation.surface: Someone is told to write down the name of an Australian town and praised for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' simply tells the solver to write the answer. BATH is the English spa city, UR the city of the Bible's Abraham, and ST (saint) the standard crossword 'good man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathurst is a regional city in New South Wales, one of Australia's oldest inland settlements.

clue.text: Champagne with mice do for lunch.?

parts.note: champagne is the bubbly, so bubble stands for it
with means and, joining two things
mice are known for the noise they make, a squeak

explanation.surface: A lunchtime party with champagne and some mice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party but means a dish. BUBBLE AND SQUEAK is a British dish of fried leftover cabbage and potato.
explanation.definitionFit: This fried mix of leftover vegetables is a traditional British meal, often eaten at lunch.

clue.text: Something very gratifying-one's easily head in composition

parts.note: a treat is something that gives great pleasure
one's is read as one is, I + S, or I'S written IS

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so it gives the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Something very satisfying, one that comes easily to the mind in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's' is I'S, written IS; 'head' takes E from the start of 'easily'.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a formal written work on a subject, a written composition.

clue.text: Perhaps Tom or Sam smashing the nucleus, not us

indicators.note: the word is smashed to pieces and its letters reassembled, minus the two letters named by not us

explanation.surface: An atom-smashing experiment run by a man named Tom or Sam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashing' scrambles NUCLEUS and 'not us' takes away U and S. Uncle Tom (of Uncle Tom's Cabin) and Uncle Sam (the US personified) are both famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Tom of Stowe's novel and Uncle Sam, the figure for the United States, are both called the brother of a parent.

clue.text: Drink, then put to bed about one, the petitioner

parts.note: to sup is to drink

indicators.note: about means around, so the bed-planting word goes around the letter for one

parts.note: to plant is to set something in a garden bed
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone drinks, then is put to bed around one in the morning, a petitioner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put to bed' sounds like going to sleep, but it means planting in a garden bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A suppliant is one who asks humbly, who begs or pleads, like someone making a formal petition.

explanation.surface: Something out of the ordinary that someone might comment on.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into REMARK-ABLE: able to be remarked on, that is, something that might be said.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unusual is striking or extraordinary; taken literally, a thing worth commenting on is one that can be voiced as a comment.

indicators.note: the work is placed at the centre of the church abbreviation, which is what 'work centre' tells us

parts.note: CE stands for the Church of England
op. (opus) is a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone struggling with jobs at a church's work centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contend with' looks like a fight, but here it means manage. CE is the Church of England; OP (opus) is a work.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage or handle a difficulty is to deal successfully with it, the same sense as contending with it.

clue.text: The end of Mr Lane? It could be

indicators.note: the letters of the name and the following word could be rearranged into the answer

parts.note: the name's letters are anagram fodder
the word's letters join the fodder

explanation.surface: A man named Lane wondering whether his death is near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' tells you the letters of MR LANE and IT could be rearranged into the answer; 'The end of' reads as a phrase about the man but the definition is just 'The end'.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminal is the final stopping point of a line or route, the end of it.

explanation.surface: A singer making people wealthier than ourselves richer still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'betters' reads as superiors but means people who bet: a treble is a bet on three races that pays out big if all three win.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy soprano in a choir sings the highest part; a three-race accumulator wager can make a punter's fortune.

clue.text: Jack Handley takes part of prince

indicators.note: the answer is only a part of the two words, a run of letters taken from inside them

explanation.surface: A man named Jack Handley acting in a play as a prince.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across jacK HANdley.
explanation.definitionFit: Khan is a title for a ruler or prince in Central Asia and in parts of the Muslim world.

clue.text: Musical instrument used for march in A—nothing unusual

indicators.note: unusual shows the letters are set in an unusual order

parts.note: nothing is zero, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: An instrument used for a march in A, nothing out of the ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in A' looks like a musical key; 'unusual' rearranges MARCH, IN, A and O (nothing).
explanation.definitionFit: A mouth organ is a small free-reed wind instrument played by blowing and drawing breath.

parts.note: Byron's poem on Sennacherib opens with a man who came down like the wolf on the fold: 'lupine' is wolfish and 'descendant' is one who comes down

explanation.surface: A wolf descended from Lord Byron's family line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Descendant' reads as offspring but means one who descends. Byron's poem 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' begins 'The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Byron's poem, the invading king from ancient Mesopotamia swoops down on Jerusalem like a wolf on sheep.

clue.text: Revolutionary painting and so on, including a saint, and birds

indicators.note: including means the two outer pieces hold the saint between them

parts.note: red is the colour of revolution and a word for a communist
painting is one of the arts
St is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: Revolutionary art, including a portrait of a saint, and some birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like an adjective for the painting, but it is RED, the colour of communism; 'including' tucks the saint inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Redstarts are small songbirds of the thrush family with red-brown tails.

clue.text: A little bit of quiet literary work

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical instruction for quiet
an article is a piece of writing in a paper or magazine

explanation.surface: A small piece of gentle writing.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the musical symbol for piano, soft.
explanation.definitionFit: A particle is a minute portion of matter, a tiny scrap.

clue.text: Armlet of metal a doctor returned

parts.note: brass is an alloy of copper and zinc

indicators.note: something returned is sent back, so the doctor abbreviation is read backwards

explanation.surface: A doctor gives back a metal bracelet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns DR into RD at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A brassard is a band worn round the upper arm, such as a mourning or identification band.

parts.note: in Morse code the letter S is sent as three short signals

explanation.surface: A man called S. Morse owns three of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'S Morse' looks like a person's initial and surname; it is the letter S in Morse code, which is three short marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Short signals in Morse code are written as small round marks, and the letter S is three of them.

clue.text: Firms combined to get vehicle rent raised

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means lifted upward, so the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to let is to rent out

explanation.surface: Companies joining forces to get the rent on a vehicle increased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' looks like a price going up, but in a down clue it turns LET upwards into TEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartel is a group of companies acting together to fix prices or limit competition, an association of businesses.

indicators.note: the concession word is returned, that is sent back, so it is read backwards

parts.note: a sop is something given to placate, a concession
set means firm, as a jelly sets

explanation.surface: A drink offered as a concession, sent back by a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a company but means solid, as a jelly sets; 'returned' turns the concession word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A posset is a hot drink of milk curdled with wine or ale.

explanation.surface: Asking whether a maker of tea leaves is a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a bush produces foliage. A shrub is also an old drink of fruit juice, sugar and rum or brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A woody plant smaller than a tree bears foliage; a cordial of fruit juice and spirits was also given this name.

explanation.surface: Where someone called Mercy is staying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mercy's' looks like a woman's name; in the old phrase 'to give quarter' quarter means mercy to a beaten enemy, so the clue reads 'Mercy is' plural as the word with an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing clemency to a defeated foe is giving quarter; soldiers' accommodation is their billet or lodging.

clue.text: River has little time to rise, one concludes

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: hr is the short form of hour, a short period of time
taken as written: one comes at the end, which concludes signals

explanation.surface: A river rises briefly before reaching its end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to rise' turns HR into RH in this down clue, and 'one concludes' puts ONE at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhône is a major European river flowing from Switzerland through France to the Mediterranean.

indicators.note: about signals that the letters are turned around into a new order

parts.note: to re-tyre a wheel is to fit a new tyre, spelt tire in old and US use, the object of re-tiring

explanation.surface: An argument about what retirement is for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel but is a line of seats. 'retirement' read as re-tire-ment makes the tire (tyre) its object; 'about' rearranges TIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is one of a series of rows or levels placed one above another, as in a theatre.

parts.note: Chester is a cathedral city in Cheshire
ton is fashion, the fashionable set, and it follows the city here

explanation.surface: A writer from the city who keeps up with fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: CHESTER is a walled city in north-west England; TON is an old word for fashion or high society.
explanation.definitionFit: G. K. Chesterton was an English author, creator of the priest-detective Father Brown.

parts.note: a day is a period of time
to break is to smash

explanation.surface: An excited exclamation that a great time was had in the early hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' looks like praise for a good time but means breaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Dawn, when light first breaks, is the start of the morning.

explanation.surface: Someone whipping a lid.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text has a stray 7 that the page does not print. The eyelid carries eyelashes, so 'lid' is the eyelid, not a cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Strokes with a whip are lashes; hairs fringing the eyelid are eyelashes.
